item.title: Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26
item.description: Whistleblower reports rise as market expands, but experts call for greater transparency, stronger safeguards and wider coverage of violations ...
item.dc:creator: Sachin P Mampatta
item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26

Whistleblower tipoffs on insider trading up sharply as Sebi gets 25 in FY26 Whistleblower reports rise as market expands, but experts call for greater transparency, stronger safeguards and wider coverage of violations premium

Sebi received 25 insider-trading tipoffs in FY26, compared with just five over the previous six financial years. (Photo: Reuters)

Sachin P Mampatta Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 11:05 PM IST

Listen to This Article

A regulatory mechanism to provide tipoffs on violations in insider trading in return for monetary rewards as high as ~10 crore may finally be showing signs of taking off.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi)   in December 2019 had established the Office of Informant Protection (OIP) to process tipoffs on insider trading. However, the response was that informants provided just five tipoffs in the first six years of the programme — from 2019-20 (FY20) to FY25.

But FY26 was different. The number of tipoffs in a single financial year increased to 25, shows the latest Annual Report, released on August 6. Fourteen of these have been concluded (including one from the previous year) while 12 were still under examination, according to the report.

This may point to the beginning of a rising role of whistleblowers in aiding stock-market policing amid the rapid expansion in capital markets in recent years.

The stock exchanges have added over 180 million investors and hundreds of companies since FY19, the last year before the establishment of the whistleblower mechanism.

The regulator added more than 300 employees since FY19 and invested in advanced technology to keep up with increased demands.

“This could possibly be a sign of increasing confidence in the reporting mechanism by potential whistleblowers with substantive information in hand to report,” noted Rohitashwa Prasad, partner at law firm Dentons Link Legal. More can be done to encourage people to come forward, he said.

According to Prasad, mature markets such as the United States (US) have limited legal delays and avoid a cap on rewards, besides providing more protection against employer retaliation.

The US Securities Exchange Commission (US SEC) announced a $279 million reward (or over ~2,000 crore, based on the prevailing exchange rate) for a tip in May 2023, shows SEC statement disclosures.

Whistleblowers whose employment is affected because of reporting violations to the regulator have stronger safeguards against retaliation, Prasad said.

“Under the Dodd Frank Act, an employee who has reported to the SEC can make a retaliation claim directly in a federal court,” he said. The SEC website tells whistleblowers facing retaliation that “you may be able to sue your employer in federal court and seek double back pay (with interest), reinstatement, reasonable attorneys’ fees, and reimbursement for certain costs in connection with the litigation”.

The Sebi regulation notes that informants facing retaliation from employers can approach competent courts or tribunals for relief. It also adds that employers found to be in violation may be liable for regulatory action, but adds that “nothing in these regulations will require the Board to direct reinstatement or compensation by an employer”.

Sumit Agrawal, founder, Regstreet Law Advisors and former Sebi officer, noted that there was limited publicly available information on the outcomes of the OIP mechanism. It can be difficult to objectively evaluate the effectiveness of the initiative without granular information on the number of informants rewarded, the number of tipoffs that resulted in investigations or enforcement proceedings, and the eventual outcomes of such proceedings, Agrawal said.

A request under the Right to Information (RTI) Act that Business Standard filed separately also did not result in additional information.

The scope of violations covered by the informant mechanism can also be expanded, according to Agrawal.

“They should consider a mechanism covering all serious security-market violations. The mechanism could include front-running, fraudulent or manipulative conduct, material disclosure violations, falsifying accounts and serious intermediary misconduct. There is no clear policy reason for an incentivised informant mechanism to remain restricted to insider trading,” Agrawal said. An email sent to the regulator did not receive a reply.

item.title: Infosys Q2 results: Net profit rises 6.2% to ₹7,823 cr, revenue up 10.7%
item.description: Net profit rises 6.2% to ₹7,823 cr, revenue up 10.2% ...
item.dc:creator: Avik Das
item.content:encoded: India’s second-largest IT services firm, Infosys, cut its revenue forecast for the financial year 2026-27 as it saw growth weaken in its largest market, the US, and an increase in AI-driven deflationary pressure on revenue. The company now expects revenue to grow between 1 and 2 per cent, down from the 1.5-3 per cent it expected three months ago. Infosys’ net profit for the second quarter rose 6.4 per cent to Rs 7,838 crore, while revenue was up 10.7 per cent to Rs 49,244 crore, helped by its financial services and energy and utilities businesses. The Q2 FY27 net profit missed analysts’ estimates, but revenue beat expectations. Analysts polled by Bloomberg expected net profit of Rs 7,904 crore and revenue of Rs 49,108 crore. On a dollar basis, revenue was up 1.3 per cent, while on a constant currency basis, it was up 1.5 per cent, which was just better than Wipro’s 0.6 per cent. It was a disappointing quarter for the Bengaluru-based company, which grew at its slowest pace in at least six quarters. On top of that, the outlook provided little room for comfort as AI-driven deflationary pressure, lower-than-expected discretionary spending going ahead, sector-specific softness and an ongoing volatile economic environment are expected to make the second half tougher than the first. “It was a soft quarter for us, the volumes were softer and in artificial intelligence (AI) we are also seeing compression. We are only taking up contracts that meet our economic guidelines,” chief executive officer (CEO) and managing director (MD) Salil Parekh said. With little visibility into large deals and sector-specific weakness, the impact was evident on Infosys’ US-listed shares, which were down almost 6.4 per cent in pre-market trading. The total contract value of large deals won during the last three months was $5.2 billion, which included a mega deal of more than $2 billion. However, the mega deal will only ramp up from the end of the financial year, and the real benefits – about 1 per cent of revenue – will kick in only from April. Such deals, which are chased by all companies, are heavily skewed towards cost optimisation and vendor consolidation projects. The challenge with such deals is that they are often slow to ramp up and take time to materialise. In a demand environment that is already subdued, large deals would also mean fierce competition among IT services players, which usually eats into margins. The positive aspect of the results was AI revenue. Infosys also said its AI revenue accounted for 10.5 per cent of its topline, up from 8.2 per cent in the first quarter, growing 29 per cent sequentially. That market opportunity, which Parekh has often touted as a $300 billion opportunity, consists of AI strategy and engineering, data for AI, process AI, agentic legacy modernisation, physical AI and AI trust. “Although operating margin remained stable at 21%, the weaker growth outlook is likely to remain the key focus for investors. If Infosys continues to rely on acquisitions to support reported growth without a meaningful recovery in its underlying business, the market could begin to assign it a lower valuation multiple,” Manav Medewala of Mirae Asset Sharekhan wrote in a note. Financial services, the main contributor to revenue, was up 2.1 per cent, while energy, utilities and resources were up 7.3 per cent. Retail, which still faces headwinds, was down 7.7 per cent, and hi-tech was down 17.3 per cent. North American revenue was down 1.5 per cent, offset by Europe, which was up 4.6 per cent. The operating margin was nearly flat at 21.1 per cent, with positive currency impacts and a higher number of working days more than offset by acquisition-related efforts. “The second half will be impacted from wage hikes and the continued intensity on pricing,” chief financial officer Jayesh Sanghrajka said. The company added 4,480 employees, and its headcount was 332,542 at the end of September. Voluntary attrition was 12.7 per cent, and it hired 8,000 freshers in the quarter.

item.title: AI-discovered software bugs may trigger more outages, warn cyber experts
item.description: Cybersecurity experts say AI is accelerating the discovery and exploitation of software flaws, raising the risk of further disruptions even as its impact on successful hacks remains uncertain ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / AI-discovered software bugs may trigger more outages, warn cyber experts

AI-discovered software bugs may trigger more outages, warn cyber experts Cybersecurity experts say AI is accelerating the discovery and exploitation of software flaws, raising the risk of further disruptions even as its impact on successful hacks remains uncertain

(Photo: Reuetrs)

Reuters 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 10:37 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruptions along the lines of the outages that spread across government websites globally this week, according to seven cybersecurity professionals who spoke to Reuters.   AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm.   Matthew Prince, the chief executive of digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare, told Reuters he was aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaced long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet.

“I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said in an interview on Thursday.   The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Wednesday happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a long-established programming language that powers a huge swathe of the internet. Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch the vulnerabilities before hackers exploited them, some simply took their sites offline until they could make them safe.

VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity. The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities in PHP alternative Node.js and streaming programme Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that Indian certificate authority eMudhra had used an extraordinarily weak cryptographic key that potentially put users across the internet at risk.   “If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.”

Timelines Shortening   The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling, and mistakes, or “bugs”, that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places.   Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks — called “exploits” — could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional.   That would, in the past, have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gradually roll out software updates.   AI has effectively thrown those assumptions out of the window.   Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny and can produce exploits in hours.

Shane Fry, the chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months had effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry.   “What's fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponize them,” Fry said.   Scary monsters   While all the experts Reuters spoke to agreed that defenders’ timelines were getting shorter, they were split on whether AI would lead to a hacker free-for-all.   Daniel Stenberg, the lead developer of the file transfer tool curl, argued that the vulnerabilities found by AI models tended to be exotic bugs that were difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of. Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks."

There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week. Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that — like Amazon and Cloudflare — it had seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said that, as of 2 p.m. Eastern Time on Thursday (1800 GMT), the cybercriminals he tracked appeared to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it.   Prince, of Cloudflare, told Reuters he had seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability.   The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house.

The confrontation might be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors was far worse.   “The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said.   Japan to simulate cyberattacks    Japan said on Friday it will set up a team to simulate  cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI) to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organisations scramble to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet. Highlighting the extent of the disruption, Japan’s third-largest mobile carrier, SoftBank, said on Friday it was suspending its emergency alert system for mobile users.That means customers will not receive early warnings for earthquakes, tsunami alerts or disaster and evacuation information.

item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / First Russian diesel shipment since 2022 heads to US under Trump-Putin deal

First Russian diesel shipment since 2022 heads to US under Trump-Putin deal A tanker carrying 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel is expected to reach New York on November 7, marking the first US import of Russian petroleum products since the 2022 ban

Dmitry Peskov, Presidential Press Secretary, Russia

Reuters 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 10:33 PM IST

Listen to This Article

A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tonnes of Russian diesel is heading towards New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday, following an agreement reached this month between Moscow and US President Donald Trump.   Trump announced the surprise deal to import Russian diesel as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.   Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.   The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low-sulphur diesel at the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7.

The identities of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022. Also Read

Trump says Musk restored Ukraine's Starlink access, dodges call question

Trump admin offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said that additional shipments will follow as Russian and US companies work out contracts for the deliveries.   Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia's sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help resolve complicated payment issues relating to the agreement.   The deal also involved Russia agreeing to lift a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.

Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter".   Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tonnes per month by year-end.   Last week, export cargoes were loaded at the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk, but their final destinations are not clear, with most tankers signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG shipping data showed.   Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Brazil and Turkey, as well as to African countries.
